bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
Neutral silver atoms pass between differently shaped pole pieces. A field that varies with position exerts a force on their magnetic moments. Two separated spots on the screen correspond to the two values of the effective spin component.

$$S_n=\pm\hbar/2$$

+++ A closer look
The force on the atom is $F_z=\mu_z\,\partial B/\partial z$: in a uniform field the magnetic moment is only turned, not pushed aside, so the pole pieces must differ in shape to make the field grow towards one side. This two-level model omits nuclear spin. High and low clicks identify the two calibrated outcomes. Only some detections are sounded so the clicks remain distinct. Look at the pole pieces in the middle of the bench. The field gradient deflects the branches gradually. The detector spacing is drawn to make them easy to separate. In a real apparatus the deflection also depends on the atom's speed and time in the field.
+++

> [Lịch sử] Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach did this experiment in 1922 in Frankfurt, sending a beam of silver atoms through the narrow gap of a magnet. On the collecting glass plate the silver formed two separate marks rather than one continuous smear. The idea of electron spin only appeared in 1925 (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit); later the two marks were understood as coming from the spin of the single outer electron of the silver atom.

> [Thử ngay] [[Send an unpolarized beam|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Select atoms that exited at plus along z. A second analyzer on the same axis sends them to plus again. The repeatability follows from the state selected at the first stage.

$$P(+z\mid+z)=1$$

+++ A closer look
Selecting the minus exit first also gives a repeatable result, this time minus. The pole colors identify the calibrated axis. This is a conditional experiment. We count only atoms transmitted by the preparation stage and exclude those blocked upstream. Comparing an unfiltered beam straight from the oven with the selected beam would compare two different ensembles.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Switch to a −z beam|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Keep the +z beam and rotate the analyzer. For an angle θ between the axes, the plus-branch amplitude is cos(θ/2). Squaring it gives the probability of reaching the plus exit.

$$P(+)=\cos^2(\theta/2),\quad P(-)=1-P(+)$$

> [Ví dụ] θ = 90° gives cos²45° = ½: the two ports are equal. θ = 60° gives cos²30° = ¾: three quarters of the atoms reach the plus port.

+++ A closer look
The probabilities sum to one because the model counts every atom at one of the two exits. Why the half-angle? The states +z and −z point in opposite directions, 180° apart in ordinary space, yet in state space they are perpendicular vectors, only «90° apart». Angles in ordinary space are therefore halved in state space, and the amplitude is cos(θ/2). Check both ends: θ = 0 gives amplitude 1, θ = 180° gives amplitude 0.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Set the analyzer transverse to z|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Drag the axis to give P(+) = 50%, within 1.4 percentage points.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Each atom still enters one of two exits. Weight each exit value by its probability and add them. The mean changes continuously as the magnet turns.

$$\langle S_n\rangle=(\hbar/2)\cos\theta$$

+++ A closer look
When three quarters of the probability is at plus, the difference between the two probabilities is one half. The mean spin component is then ħ/4. If someone reports measuring ħ/4 on one atom with this apparatus, ask where the number came from. It could be an average over many readings from both branches. A single detection corresponds to one of the two eigenvalues of the spin component.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Compare with aligned axes|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the axis to predict 75% at plus, within 1.4 percentage points.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: Compare 0° with 90°, then try a value in between.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Turning the analyzer through half a turn swaps the positions of its exits. A +z atom gives minus with certainty if the measurement axis points along −z. Compare the probability display with the detector positions.

$$P(+;180^\circ)=0$$

+++ A closer look
Reduce the angle from 180° and the plus signal returns. The spots are labeled relative to the analyzer being used. Imagine watching a fixed screen while the axis and its exit labels rotate together. A position on the screen alone does not assign a plus or minus sign. You need the exit calibration at the time of the measurement. For this reason both the angle and the preparation belong in the lab notebook.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Set the axis to 180°|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: Drag until P(+) is 25%, within 1.4 percentage points.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: Take the supplement of the angle that gave 75%.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Prepare −z at the source. For the same analyzer direction the probabilities exchange places compared with +z. The mean changes sign.

$$P(+\mid-z)=\sin^2(\theta/2)$$

+++ A closer look
On a perpendicular axis, both preparations give equal probabilities. Measuring along z on identically prepared atoms distinguishes the two cases. Keep the analyzer fixed and select each exit of the preparation filter in turn. Collect many atoms at each setting and normalize each record separately. The plus fraction for the first preparation should match the minus fraction for the second within statistical uncertainty.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Switch to +z|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Mix equal amounts of +z and −z without retaining their labels. Average the two probabilities because the atoms were prepared in different ways. Every analyzer angle gives equal probabilities at the two exits.

$$P_{\rm mix}(+)=\tfrac12[\cos^2(\theta/2)+\sin^2(\theta/2)]=\tfrac12$$

+++ A closer look
A pure +z preparation also splits equally at one particular angle. Several measurement directions help distinguish the preparations. The distinction lies in the preparation. In the filtered beam every atom has the same quantum state. For the mixture the source selects either state for each atom and discards that label. Combining those two sets of events removes the polarization in the average.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Test the mixture along z|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
Set an angle, let atoms accumulate, then compare the observed fraction with the predicted probability. Changing the angle starts a new count because the distribution changes.

$$f_+=N_+/(N_++N_-)$$

+++ A closer look
In a short run the observed fraction may differ considerably from the probability. For independent trials its standard error is $\sqrt{f(1-f)/N}$: with N = 100 and f = 0.5 it is about 0.05; halving the error takes four times as many counts. The red bar on the graph shows this error. Record the angle, preparation, plus count and total arrivals. Start a separate line for each new angle. Combine records only when their conditions match; pooling several angles could hide the angular dependence you are looking for.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Start a run at 90°|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: The incident beam is prepared along +z.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: Average over many atoms prepared in +z.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: One measurement yields one of these values along n.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: For a +z beam and a magnet at 90°, what happens?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: P(+) = cos²(90°/2) = cos²45° = ½. Each atom still enters one of the two ports, +ħ/2 or −ħ/2; none goes straight through the middle even though the mean is zero.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: A transverse measurement gives the same statistics for +z and an equal mixture. What can distinguish them?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: Along z the +z state always exits at plus, while the equal mixture still splits equally.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: For a +z beam at 60°, what fraction goes to minus?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Why does the magnet need a field gradient?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: To produce a separating force on magnetic moments
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: To give neutral atoms electric charge
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: The moment’s potential energy depends on the local field, so a spatial variation produces a separating force.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Why does a near-zero transverse mean not establish that the beam is unpolarized?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.dap: Pure +z also has zero transverse mean. Prepare fresh atoms identically and measure along z: pure +z always gives the same sign, whereas an equal mixture gives the signs equally often.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: Intrinsic angular momentum of a quantum system.
bai.moTa: Rotate the magnet to change the measurement axis and count atoms at both exits.
bai.yChinh: Measuring one component of an atomic beam with effective spin ½ gives two outcomes. The angle between the preparation and measurement axes determines their probabilities.
bai.giaiThich: The oven on the left emits silver atoms. The preparation stage is a small z-axis magnet plus a plate: with one hole blocked only the +z or −z beam passes, with both open the beam is an even mixture. The gold arrow is the prepared spin direction, the orange-red arrow the measurement axis n of the analyzing magnet. The screen keeps a mark for every atom; the two columns on the right compare the counted fractions with the theoretical probability (gold bar). Sizes, deflections and flight speed are enlarged or slowed; after the preparation stage the beam is drawn back to the centre for clarity.
bai.conSo.1: At 60° a +z beam gives 75% at the plus exit.
bai.hieuDung: Spin is not a tiny ball spinning on its own. It is intrinsic angular momentum, not matter turning about an axis. The two spots show that measuring one spin component has only two outcomes; a single spot does not tell us what a measurement along a different axis would have yielded.
bai.nguon: Written by Trí Lữ. W. Gerlach and O. Stern, Zeitschrift für Physik 9 (1922), 349. Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. III, Chapter 6, Spin One-Half.
